cards.heading: The problem
cards.body: Hosts have a single default gateway. If that router fails, they lose everything off their subnet, even when a second router is right there. A first hop redundancy protocol (FHRP) lets two or more routers share a virtual IP and virtual MAC that hosts use as their gateway.

cards.heading: HSRP active and standby
cards.body: HSRP (Cisco) elects one active router, which answers for the virtual IP and MAC, and one standby router ready to take over. Hellos go every 3 seconds; the standby takes over if it hears nothing for 10 (hold time). Hosts notice nothing: the gateway's IP and MAC stay the same.
cards.example:
Virtual IP 10.1.1.1 / 0000.0c07.ac01
   R1 .2 (active)        R2 .3 (standby)
          \                /
               [SW1]
             PCs: gateway 10.1.1.1

cards.heading: Election
cards.body: Highest priority wins (default 100, range 0-255). If priorities tie, the highest interface IP wins.
cards.example:
interface g0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.2 255.255.255.0
 standby 1 ip 10.1.1.1
 standby 1 priority 110

cards.heading: Preempt
cards.body: HSRP doesn't take the active role from a working active router, even if a router with a higher priority joins later, unless that router has 'standby 1 preempt'. Without preempt, whoever came up first stays active.

cards.heading: Interface tracking
cards.body: If the active router's uplink fails, it still answers hosts but can't forward their traffic anywhere useful. Tracking lowers its priority when the tracked interface goes down, so a peer with preempt takes over. The decrement must push it below the peer.

cards.heading: Virtual MACs
cards.body: HSRPv1 uses 0000.0c07.acXX and HSRPv2 0000.0c9f.fXXX, where X is the group number in hex. HSRPv2 supports groups 0-4095 and IPv6.

cards.heading: VRRP and GLBP
cards.body: VRRP is the open standard (RFC 5798): master and backup routers, preempt on by default, and the virtual IP may be a real router's address. GLBP (Cisco) load-balances: one active virtual gateway (AVG) hands out different virtual MACs so several forwarders (AVFs) share the traffic.
